opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core of it comes down to the size of the prize and the structure of the uncertainty. If you take seriously the possibility that AI systems could eventually automate a large share of the tasks humans currently do in the economy, then you're talking about capturing a meaningful fraction of world output, which is on the order of a hundred trillion dollars a year. Even if you assign a modest probability to that outcome, the expected value of being positioned for it is enormous relative to the tens or even hundreds of billions currently being spent on data centers and chips.

The second piece is that compute infrastructure has long lead times. You can't decide one morning that you need a gigawatt-scale cluster and have it the next quarter. You need to secure power, permits, land, cooling, chip supply from a very concentrated supply chain, and the networking to tie it together. That can take years. So if you wait until the returns are obvious and already showing up in revenue, you're too late. Your competitors who built ahead of demand will have the capacity and you won't. It's a bit like building railways or electrical grids: the investment has to precede the usage it enables.

Third, there's a feedback loop that I think people underappreciate. Scaling up compute has been one of the most reliable drivers of capability improvements we've seen, and better capabilities unlock new applications, which generate revenue, which funds more compute. Investing early isn't just betting on future returns. It's partly what creates those returns, because it moves you along the capability curve faster.

And finally, there's the option value. Building capacity early gives you the flexibility to train larger models, to serve inference at scale if demand takes off, and to experiment. If things turn out more slowly than hoped, some of that capital is underutilized for a while, and that's a real cost. But the downside is bounded, whereas the upside of being under-provisioned during a period of really rapid AI-driven growth is that you simply miss it. When you weigh a bounded downside against a potentially very large upside, investing ahead of demand looks pretty rational, even if it looks like overbuilding from the perspective of today's revenues.

r001.rationale: It explains that compute capacity takes years to build and requires securing power, permits, land, chips, and networking, so waiting until returns are clear can leave firms too late to expand.

r002.rationale: It warns that under-provisioning may cause firms to miss rapid growth, but does not predict a later investment frenzy.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core reason is that the investment decision isn't really about today's revenue; it's about the expected size of the market once the systems are capable enough to automate a large share of economically valuable work. If you take seriously the idea that AI could eventually substitute for a meaningful fraction of human labor, then the relevant comparison is against global labor compensation, which is on the order of sixty or seventy trillion dollars a year. Even capturing a few percent of that is an enormous prize, and a few hundred billion a year in capex looks modest relative to it.

The second piece is that compute is a long-lead-time input. Building fabs, data centers, power, and cooling takes years, so if you wait until the demand is unambiguously visible, you're structurally late. In that kind of race, being a year or two behind on capacity can mean losing the frontier, and the frontier is where most of the value seems to accrue. So firms are effectively buying an option: they pay now to be positioned if the scaling trends continue, and the historical regularity of those trends makes that option look reasonably priced.

Third, there's a feedback loop that justifies front-loading. Better models generate revenue, but they also lower the cost of producing the next generation, through things like synthetic data, automated research assistance, and more efficient inference. If you believe in even a modest version of that loop, the returns to early investment are compounding rather than linear, and the standard discounting intuition undersells them.

Now, I'd add the obvious caveat: this reasoning is sensitive to whether the capability trends actually hold and whether adoption is as fast as the labs hope. If progress stalls or diffusion into the real economy is much slower than expected, a lot of this capital will have been deployed too early and you'd see a correction, which has happened with other general-purpose technologies like railways and fiber. But the asymmetry matters. The downside is a painful but bounded write-down; the upside is being one of the firms that owns the infrastructure for what could be the largest economic transition in history. Given that payoff structure, investing well ahead of visible returns is, I think, the rational bet, even if it's not a certain one.

r001.rationale: The response says compute infrastructure takes years to build and that waiting until demand is visible leaves firms late, but it does not explain avoiding the adjustment costs of rapidly expanding capacity later.

r002.rationale: The response warns that insufficient or delayed capacity could leave firms behind, but it does not predict that underinvestment will trigger a later investment frenzy.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key is that you’re investing in a stream of future returns, rather than expecting the investment to pay for itself immediately. A large upfront investment can make economic sense if the expected future revenues are sufficiently large, even after you discount them for the time you have to wait and the risk that they don’t materialize.

And compute infrastructure takes time to build. You need to secure power, construct data centers, and install the hardware. If you wait until the demand is already there, you might be years behind. So there’s value in having capacity available when it becomes useful, both to train models and to serve customers.

Of course, that doesn’t mean any amount of spending is justified. Chips can become obsolete, demand might grow more slowly than expected, and improvements in efficiency could change how much compute you need. The economic case is that the potential returns are large enough to compensate for those risks and the cost of committing capital early.

r001.rationale: The response says early capacity avoids being years behind when demand arrives, but it does not explain that early investment avoids the adjustment costs of rapidly expanding later.

r002.rationale: It notes that demand could outpace available capacity, but does not predict that insufficient current investment may trigger a later investment frenzy.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the basic reason is that building the infrastructure takes time. If you wait until the demand is already there and the returns are obvious, you can’t instantly produce the chips, data centers, power connections, and everything else you need. You have to make those investments in advance.

And the relevant economic question isn’t whether you’re earning revenue immediately. It’s whether the expected future returns justify the upfront cost, accounting for the delay and the risk. If you expect AI systems to become much more useful, then having the compute available when that happens could be very valuable.

Of course, that doesn’t mean every investment will pay off. You could overestimate demand, or the hardware could become obsolete more quickly than you expected. But the fact that spending precedes revenue isn’t, by itself, evidence that the investment is irrational. That’s a normal feature of building infrastructure.

r001.rationale: It says infrastructure takes time and that investing in advance avoids waiting until demand arrives, when capacity cannot be produced instantly. This communicates avoiding the costs and constraints of rapid later expansion.

r002.rationale: It discusses the risk of waiting to invest, but does not predict that insufficient current investment may trigger a later investment frenzy.
